hard_phrases: it is important to note that
it is crucial to remember that

regex_structures.name: participle_tail
regex_structures.description: Comma + present-participle tail that adds interpretation without new information. Narrowed 2026-09-18: 'setting' and 'marking' were dropped because their attested forms ('setting the stage for', 'marking a pivotal moment') are already BS-004, and their bare forms are ordinary English ('setting aside his bread and butter'). 'reflecting' and 'emphasizing' are now scoped to an abstract complement, since the human uses take a concrete one ('reflecting the clouds', 'emphasizing each slow down-stroke'). Measured 1.9 to 0.0 per 10k on 47,088 sentences of long-form human prose, with recall on the attested tell unchanged.
regex_structures.fix: Delete the dangling -ing clause, or commit to the interpretation in its own sentence.

regex_structures.name: significance_puffery
regex_structures.description: Inflated framing of mundane facts as sweeping historical claims.

detection.pattern: \b(marking a (pivotal|crucial|defining|key) (moment|chapter)|setting the stage for|part of a broader (movement|trend|effort) to|underscores its enduring (significance|importance))\b

regex_structures.fix: Strip the editorializing and state what actually happened.

regex_structures.name: negative_parallelism
regex_structures.description: 'not just X, but also Y' contrast inflation, plus the explicit 'not only X but also Y' correlative. Narrowed 2026-09-18: the previous pattern accepted any 'not only ... but' and fired 94 times, 20.0 per 10k, on 47,088 sentences of long-form human prose, 93 of them on the ordinary correlative ('I was not only instructed in everything, but was soon engaged in helping'). The narrowed form fires 7 times, 1.5 per 10k, with the attested AP-006 tell intact. The bare correlative used as a flourish ('not only a design problem but a cultural one') is no longer detected and is carried by the self_review antithesis item.
regex_structures.fix: State the point directly with a simple conjunction.

regex_structures.name: despite_faces_challenges
regex_structures.description: 'Despite its X, [subject] faces challenges...' hedge-praise formula.
regex_structures.fix: Replace with specific problems and specific responses; drop the framing formula.

regex_structures.name: that_clause_subject
regex_structures.description: Sentence opening with a 'That ... is' clausal subject.
regex_structures.fix: Move the evidence/source to the front; let the claim follow.

regex_structures.name: x_not_y_contrastive
regex_structures.description: Copula-anchored 'X, not Y' contrastive binary that reads constructed: a copula (is/was/are/were/means/becomes/remains), a short noun phrase, a comma, then a Y that closes the clause. Narrowed 2026-09-18 from a bare two-token pattern that fired 358 times, 76.0 per 10k, on 47,088 sentences of long-form human prose. Known and accepted false positive: the identical shape serves as a scope note or a factual correction ("The self-review rubric is data, not code.", "The response was 406, not 421."). Nothing readable in the string separates that sense from the tell, so a firing on it is justified rather than rewritten. Contrastives outside this frame are no longer detected and are carried by the self_review rubric.
regex_structures.fix: Make the positive claim and let it stand, or use a separate sentence for the contrast.

regex_structures.name: negation_flip_antithesis
regex_structures.description: Two-sentence copula flip: 'X is not Y. It is Z.' The single most characteristic antithesis of LLM prose. A two-sentence relative of BS-006 ('not just X but Y') and BS-011 ('X, not Y'), which the single-sentence checks miss.
regex_structures.fix: Make the positive claim and let it stand. Do not negate an alternative in one sentence and flip to the real point in the next.
regex_structures.research_basis: Named the LLM's single most-favored rhetorical move ('it's not X; it's Y') in the Dead Language Society rhetorical analysis (2025); corroborates proposed-rules #5.

regex_structures.name: rarely_flip_aphorism
regex_structures.description: A disguised antithesis: a copula claim hedged with rarely/seldom/never, then flipped to the 'real' point in a second copula sentence. 'The interesting move is rarely the new automation. It is deciding what to leave alone.'
regex_structures.fix: Drop the 'is rarely X. It is Y' flip; state plainly what the point or the work actually was.

regex_structures.name: wh_cleft_pronouncement
regex_structures.description: A pseudo-cleft fronted by a 'What ...' clause pivoting on a copula into a noun, used for portentous effect: 'What matters here is the design.' Sibling of the that-clause subject (BS-010).
regex_structures.fix: Make the plain claim. Drop the 'What ... is ...' framing and lead with the thing itself.
regex_structures.research_basis: proposed-rules #1; scoped to declaratives (interrogatives end in '?' and do not match).

regex_structures.name: meta_framing_opener
regex_structures.description: Opening a passage by announcing its own thesis abstractly: 'The point of the redesign is ...', 'The key here is ...'. Over-signals structure before showing the concrete thing.
regex_structures.fix: Lead with the concrete thing and let the reader infer the point. Cut the 'The point of X is' scaffolding.
regex_structures.research_basis: proposed-rules #6.

regex_structures.name: disclaimer_reversal
regex_structures.description: A disclaiming sentence ('I won't claim/pretend/promise ...') immediately followed by a short emphatic 'But ...' reversal. Inter-sentential relative of BS-013; the single-sentence antithesis checks miss it.
regex_structures.fix: State what you can stand behind, plainly, in one move. Drop the disclaimer-then-flip rhythm.
regex_structures.research_basis: proposed-rules PR2-#2; in-the-wild audit 2026-06-28.

regex_structures.name: locative_pseudocleft
regex_structures.description: A pseudo-cleft pivoting on where/when/how rather than 'what' ('The gap between those two facts was where the work got lost.'). Sibling of BS-015. Scoped to an article-led noun-phrase subject so demonstrative/expletive forms ('This is how', 'Here is where', 'That was when') do not trip it.
regex_structures.fix: Lead with the subject doing the thing: 'Work got lost in that gap.' Drop the 'X is where ...' frame.
regex_structures.research_basis: proposed-rules PR2-#5; in-the-wild audit 2026-06-28. Pattern tightened from the proposed bare 'is/was where' to an article-led subject to suppress 'This is how' / 'Here is where' false positives.

regex_structures.name: noun_participle_fragment
regex_structures.description: A verbless 'Noun, past-participle.' sentence: a determiner-led noun phrase, a comma, and a trailing past participle, ending there ('The same board, rebuilt.', 'The homepage, reimagined.'). Past-participle sibling of BS-005 (present-participle tail). Bounded to a sentence-initial determiner with the participle as the final token, so it fires only on the verbless fragment, never on full clauses ('He left the room, defeated.', 'The board, which we rebuilt, is live.').
regex_structures.fix: Give it a subject and a finite verb ('We rebuilt the same board.'), or fold the participle into the neighboring sentence. Drop the noun-comma-participle fragment.
regex_structures.research_basis: In-the-wild reviewer feedback 2026-07-03 on prose that had passed the checker clean: 'The same board, rebuilt.' flagged as the 'Noun, past-participle.' construction. Scoped to a sentence-initial determiner-led NP with the participle as the terminal token to preserve the fragment guarantee and suppress false positives; the [a-z]{3,}ed floor excludes short -ed look-alikes (red/bed/shed), and the missing comma keeps fixed idioms ('Case closed.') quiet.

regex_structures.name: meta_label
regex_structures.description: A standalone meta-label line or heading that names the artifact's own format or length instead of its subject ('In 200 words', 'In brief', 'At a high level', 'To put it simply'). The mechanizable slice of the performative-framing beat: a self-aware flourish that performs concision or structure rather than carrying content. Fires ONLY when the label IS the whole bounded line/sentence (optionally one terminal mark, then a line break or end), so embedded uses ('At a high level, the system does X.') never match. TL;DR is deliberately excluded (common and acceptable in casual writing). The judgment sub-forms, self-satisfied closers, first-person meta-commentary, paradox-substitution headlines, are the self_review 'performative framing beat' rubric item, not this detector.
regex_structures.fix: Replace the format/length/brevity label with a phrase about the content itself, or cut it and let the section's content name it. Do not announce structure; let the structure be the structure.
regex_structures.research_basis: In-the-wild reviewer feedback 2026-07-06 on prose run through the humanizer: meta labels ('in 200 words', 'the reading, in brief') survived as self-aware flourishes. Scoped to a standalone bounded label with a terminal-only trailing guard so the embedding-prone phrases ('at a high level', 'to put it simply') fire only as labels, never mid-sentence. Sibling of the closer detector BS-018; the judgment sub-forms live in the self_review rubric. Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-06-performative-framing-beat-design.md.

regex_structures.name: validation_reassurance
regex_structures.description: Unsolicited second-person reassurance in a fixed frame ('You're not alone.', 'You're not imagining it.', 'You're not broken.', 'It's not just you.'). The single most-cited NEW 2026 AI tell: the model switches into therapeutic validation that reads as bizarre in most content (business posts, docs, marketing). High-precision because it matches only the 'you're not <predicate>' / 'it's not just you' frames, so ordinary negations ('You're not sure yet.', 'You are not authorized.') never match. Legitimate in genuine supportive/empathetic writing, which is why it is checklist (rewrite or justify), never hard.

detection.pattern: \byou(?:['’]re| are) not\s+(?:alone|broken|crazy|failing|imagining|overreacting|weak|the only one)\b|\bit(?:['’]s| is) not just you\b

regex_structures.fix: Cut the reassurance, or replace it with the specific thing you actually want to say. If the piece genuinely calls for empathy, make it concrete rather than a canned 'you're not X' formula.
regex_structures.research_basis: Forbes, 'The 15 New Giveaway Signs Of AI-Generated Content' (2026-02-03): AI switching into unsolicited validation ('You're not imagining it', 'You're not alone', 'You're not broken') flagged as the standout new tell, incongruous in business/productivity content. Frame-scoped to keep false positives near zero.

regex_structures.name: vague_authority_attribution
regex_structures.description: An appeal to an unnamed authority as evidence ('Researchers say...', 'Studies show...', 'Experts agree...', 'It is widely believed...', 'Many argue...'). A content-level AI tell distinct from credibility_insistence (which flags reality-assertion words like real/actual): here the sentence borrows authority it never names. The verb list is scoped to epistemic-claim frames, so a named or specific reference with a concrete action ('The researchers at MIT published their data') does not match. Checklist because attributed uses are legitimate, the fix is to name the source or cut the appeal. A news headline's trailing attribution ('Not a recession, but close, economists say': a comma, a group noun, say or says, and the end of the line with no full stop) is declined, because the story names the sources and the headline convention leaves them out; the same frame with a full stop is body prose and still fires (2026-11-09, found by the terse-register set).
regex_structures.fix: Name who: cite the specific study, person, or body, and link or reference it. If you cannot name a source, drop the claim or state it as your own view.
regex_structures.research_basis: Wikipedia 'Signs of AI writing' (2026): 'vague attributions', attributing claims to undefined authorities ('researchers', 'observers', 'scholarship') without naming them, listed as a core content tell. Scoped to unnamed-agent + epistemic-verb frames so named/specific references pass.

regex_structures.name: question_fragment_cadence
regex_structures.description: The 'The best part? It's this.' rhetorical tic: a sentence-initial determiner-led noun-phrase fragment ending in '?', immediately answered by a short sentence ('The result? A total win.', 'My advice? Take the job.'). Named repeatedly as a 2026 ChatGPT fingerprint (the 'contrasting question with a short answer' pattern). Scoped to a determiner-led NP of up to three words so WH-questions ('What is the best part?') and mid-sentence questions ('Did you see the result?') never match, the determiner must sit at a sentence boundary.
regex_structures.fix: State the point as a declarative sentence. If the setup-and-payoff is earned, use it once; repeated question-fragment beats read as a tic.
regex_structures.research_basis: Walter Writes / PlusAI 'most overused ChatGPT patterns' (2026) and in-the-wild reports: 'contrasting questions with short answers' ('The best part? It's this. The kicker? It's that.') as a durable 2026 structural fingerprint. NP-fragment + boundary scoping keeps genuine questions clear.

regex_structures.name: when_it_comes_to_opener
regex_structures.description: The 'When it comes to X...' sentence opener, a very-high-frequency AI phrase frame that sets up a topic with an empty preamble instead of stating the point. Scoped to a sentence boundary with a trailing comma so mid-sentence uses ('she knew when it comes to a vote') never match.
regex_structures.fix: Cut the preamble and state the point. 'When it comes to pricing, we keep it simple' becomes 'Our pricing is simple.'
regex_structures.research_basis: Bloomberry 'AI Sentence DNA' (2026): 'when it comes to' listed Very High across all models. Boundary plus trailing-comma scoping keeps false positives near zero.

regex_structures.name: world_state_opener
regex_structures.description: The grand temporal/world-state opener ('In a world where...', 'In an era of...', 'In an age where...', 'In a time of...'), a very-high-frequency AI hook that opens on a sweeping generalization. Complements the flagged transition 'In today's rapidly evolving' and BS-016 meta_framing_opener. Scoped to a sentence boundary and a fixed determiner-plus-noun-plus-where/of skeleton so a literal 'in a world of magic' mid-sentence never matches.

detection.pattern: (?:^|[.!?]\s+|\n)(?:in (?:a world where|an era (?:of|where)|an age (?:of|where)|a time (?:of|where))|(?:imagine|picture) a world where)\b

regex_structures.fix: Cut the cosmic setup and open on the specific. Say what is changing and for whom.
regex_structures.research_basis: Bloomberry 'AI Sentence DNA' (2026): 'In a world where...' hook formula, Very High across all models. Boundary scoping keeps mid-sentence literal uses clear.

regex_structures.name: pivotal_role_frame
regex_structures.description: The 'plays a [pivotal/crucial/key/central...] role in' template. The evaluative adjectives are individually flagged, but the template slips through when the adjective is an un-flagged option (key/central/major), so the frame itself is matched. Restricted to evaluative adjectives so a neutral 'play a supporting role in the film' does not match.
regex_structures.fix: Say what the thing actually does. 'Monitoring plays a pivotal role in catching problems' becomes 'Monitoring catches problems early.'
regex_structures.research_basis: Bloomberry 'AI Sentence DNA' (2026) and 2026 overused-phrase lists: 'play a pivotal/crucial role in' as a recurring filler template. Adjective allow-list keeps neutral role-descriptions clear.

regex_structures.name: solution_pivot
regex_structures.description: The 'That's where X comes in.' marketing pivot-to-product beat ('This is where we come in.'). Scoped to a sentence-initial 'that's/this is where' plus a terminal 'comes in.' so the idiom 'comes in handy' and ordinary locatives ('this is where we live') never match.
regex_structures.fix: State what the product does directly instead of staging a reveal.
regex_structures.research_basis: Bloomberry 'AI Sentence DNA' (2026): the reveal/solution-pivot cadence. Terminal scoping ('comes in.') keeps 'comes in handy' and locatives clear.

regex_structures.name: empathy_conditional_opener
regex_structures.description: The 'If you've ever struggled with...' empathy opener, a fixed second-person conditional that manufactures relatability, in the same family as BS-023 validation_reassurance. Scoped to a sentence boundary plus 'you've/you have ever' plus an empathy verb (struggled/wondered/felt/...), so anecdotal openers ('If you've ever been to Paris') and mid-sentence uses do not match.
regex_structures.fix: Open on the concrete situation, not a canned 'if you've ever felt X' hook.
regex_structures.research_basis: Bloomberry 'AI Sentence DNA' (2026): empathy opener 'If you've ever struggled with...'. Empathy-verb allow-list plus boundary scoping keeps genuine conditional anecdotes clear.

regex_structures.name: metaphorical_carry
regex_structures.description: Metaphorical 'carry': the fixed abstract collocation ('the design carries the weight', 'carrying the burden of the argument') and the text-unit intransitive ('eight words to carry'). A strong Claude-register tell: the verb performs gravity while no one does anything. FP-guarded by an abstract-object allow-list and, on the intransitive branch, a text-unit head noun, so literal carrying ('too heavy to carry', 'carry the groceries', 'the truck carries the load') never matches. 'load' and 'freight' were dropped from the object list during design because logistics prose uses them literally. Known accepted boundary: the fixed idiom 'carries the weight of the world' does fire; at gate=checklist that is a rewrite-or-justify prompt, and the idiom is a cliche worth a second look either way. Deliberately NOT a bare 'carry' word-flag: 'carry' is a high-frequency ordinary verb and a bare flag is the flow_over_surface_features low-ceiling trap. The wider family (any abstract noun as subject of 'carry') is not mechanizable without a parser and lives in the self_review abstraction-as-agent item.
regex_structures.fix: Name the actual agent and the actual effect. 'The layout carries the weight of the argument' -> 'The layout is what makes the argument land.' For the label form, say what the words must do: 'Eight words to carry' -> 'Eight words, and they have to do the whole job.'
regex_structures.research_basis: In-the-wild report (2026-08-06) plus caveats.json metrics_do_not_apply_to_label_text (2026-08-03), which recorded 'Eight words to carry' as a genuine AI-register tell that the checker missed.

regex_structures.name: honestly_fragment_opener
regex_structures.description: A standalone one-word interrogative opener promising candour and delivering a platitude ('Honestly? Most people don't follow up.'). Scoped to a fixed adverb set as the WHOLE bounded fragment at a sentence or line boundary, so quoted dialogue ('"Honestly?" she said.') and mid-sentence uses never match.
regex_structures.fix: Delete the fragment and state the claim. If the point is not actually candid or contrarian, the opener is advertising something the sentence does not deliver.
regex_structures.research_basis: Forbes, 'The 15 New Giveaway Signs Of AI-Generated Content' (2026-02-03), tell #3: "'Honestly?' followed by nothing honest".

regex_structures.name: quiet_prestige_modifier
regex_structures.description: The 'everything is quietly something' tic: 'quiet confidence', 'quiet rebellion', 'quietly reshaping'. Both branches are allow-listed ('quiet' + an abstract-quality noun, or 'quietly' + a transformation verb), so ordinary use ('a quiet room', 'she quietly closed the door') passes. This is the collocation, not the word: a bare 'quiet' flag was rejected on 2026-07-13 as the flow_over_surface_features trap, and that rejection stands.
regex_structures.fix: Cut the modifier or replace it with the evidence. 'Quiet confidence' -> say what the person did that showed it. 'Quietly reshaping the industry' -> name the change and who noticed.
regex_structures.research_basis: Forbes (2026-02-03), tell #5: 'Everything is quietly something', 'quiet confidence', 'quiet rebellion', 'quietly growing', 'the quiet truth'.

regex_structures.name: concessive_balance_hedge
regex_structures.description: The risk-averse both-sides frame that concludes nothing: 'While X has benefits, it also carries risks.' Scoped so BOTH the hedge verb and its object are allow-listed, leaving ordinary concessive 'While' clauses clear. Distinct frame from BS-007 ('despite ... faces ... challenges').
regex_structures.fix: Pick the claim you actually want to make and make it. If the trade-off is real, name the specific cost and who pays it, rather than balancing the sentence for its own sake.
regex_structures.research_basis: Gibson, 'The Predictable Rhetoric of AI-Generated Text' (Medium, 2026-04), device #3 'Balancing Hedging'; corroborated by Forbes tell #13 'faux balance without consequence'.

regex_structures.name: internal_cross_reference
regex_structures.description: Over-tidy self-reference: 'As mentioned above', 'As we discussed earlier', 'As noted previously'. Legitimate in long technical and academic documents, which is why it is checklist (rewrite or justify), never hard.
regex_structures.fix: Cut it and restate the point in three words, or trust the reader to remember. Keep it only where a real document needs a genuine back-reference.
regex_structures.research_basis: Forbes (2026-02-03), tell #14: 'internal references that are too tidy'.

regex_structures.name: deepening_invitation
regex_structures.description: The therapeutic prompt to go deeper: 'Let that sink in.', 'Do you want to sit with that for a while?', 'Are you ready to go deeper?', 'Read that again.' A fixed phrase set rather than a productive frame, so precision is near-total. Family relative of BS-023 (validation_reassurance).
regex_structures.fix: Delete it. If the point deserves weight, give it weight with a fact or a consequence, not an instruction to feel something.
regex_structures.research_basis: Forbes (2026-02-03), tell #7: 'questions designed to deepen', 'Do you want to sit with that for a while?', 'Are you ready to go deeper?'

regex_structures.name: withheld_insight_teaser
regex_structures.description: The setup that announces a payoff it rarely delivers: 'Here's the kicker', 'the part most people miss', 'what nobody tells you'. Scoped to the 'most people|nobody|no one' + 'miss|get wrong|tell you|know' skeleton plus the fixed 'here's the kicker'. Adjacent to 'Here's the thing', which was rejected on 2026-07-25 as register-dependent; that rejection stands; what is flagged here is the marker PLUS the withheld-insight claim.
regex_structures.fix: Lead with the insight itself. If it is genuinely counterintuitive the reader will notice without being told to.
regex_structures.research_basis: Forbes (2026-02-03), tells #1 'announcing the good part' ('Here's the kicker') and #4 'setup phrases that don't deliver' ('Here's the part most people miss').

regex_structures.name: appended_wh_label
regex_structures.description: The label line that appends a second, evaluative element promising significance instead of naming a subject: 'Method, and why this one', 'The rebuild, and why it took nine months', 'The rollout, and how we got here'. The heading states the topic, then annexes a WH clause that pre-announces the defence the body is about to make. Mechanized slice of the performative framing beat. Four FP guards keep it label-scoped: the appendix must END the bounded line (so mid-sentence coordination cannot match), the head is blocked from containing a subject pronoun or auxiliary (so an ordinary prose clause cannot match), the head is capped at 12 tokens, and the tail is short and comma-free (so a full second clause cannot match). The open-ended sibling that appends a reduced relative clause rather than a WH word ('..., and the officer the whole system turns on.') is deliberately NOT mechanized: separating it from ordinary coordination needs a parser, so it is a self_review judgment item.
regex_structures.fix: Cut the appendix. Name the subject and let the section make its own case: 'Method, and why this one' is 'Method'. If the justification is worth stating, it is worth a sentence in the body, not a promise in the label.
regex_structures.research_basis: In-the-wild reviewer report (2026-08-08) on a document that passed the 2026-08-06 checker clean: the shape fired twice in one piece, which is the durable signal (a repeated rhetorical shape) rather than any single instance.

regex_structures.name: not_but_fragment
regex_structures.description: The sentence-initial antithesis fragment: 'Not because the person stopped mattering, but because the officer is reachable.', 'Not to save time, but to save arguments.', 'Not a strategy, but a habit.' Fragment sibling of BS-013, which only covers the two-sentence copula flip ('It is not just X. It is Y.') and therefore missed this, the more common written form. The FP guard is PARALLELISM: the same function word must open both limbs (because/because, to/to, a/a), which is what separates the rhetorical fragment from ordinary prose where 'Not' heads a real subject ('Not all of them agreed, but most did.') or where the correlative sits mid-sentence ('He did not go to the store, but to the park.'), neither of which can match. The bare adverb form ('Not always, but often.') is deliberately NOT matched: without a shared function word it cannot be told from ordinary casual speech ('Not bad, but okay.'), and cry-wolf costs more than the miss.
regex_structures.fix: State the reason that holds and drop the one that does not. The rejected half is usually a claim nobody made, so cutting it costs nothing: 'Not because the person stopped mattering, but because the officer is reachable' is 'The officer is the reachable point in the system.'
regex_structures.research_basis: In-the-wild reviewer report (2026-08-08). Same document as BS-038; the reviewer named the 'Not X, but Y' structure and the checker returned nothing for it, confirming the BS-013 scope gap.

regex_structures.name: artifact_subject_carry
regex_structures.description: An artifact or document noun as the subject of 'carry' with an informational object: 'the deck carries one still of the dashboard', 'each board carries its own title, rule and legend', 'the margin rail carries the tags', 'slide 18 carries the business model', 'the presenter notes carry the argument'. The middle slice between BS-031, which matches only the fixed abstract collocations ('carries the weight|burden|meaning'), and the open abstract-subject family that stays a self_review item for want of a parser. It is mechanizable because both ends are closed lists. Detection requires BOTH an artifact-noun subject head immediately before the verb (deck, slide, board, page, section, rail, panel, frame, column, caption, chart, table, screen, dashboard, prototype, report, layout, card, note...) AND an informational object head (title, legend, argument, tags, model, lessons, story, data, still, screenshot, claim, stakes...), which is what keeps the many load-bearing homographs literal: 'the column carries the roof', 'the frame carries the glass', 'the table carries the plates' and 'the truck carries the load' all pass, because no physical-load object is in the list. Objects the subject genuinely bears in the physical world were left out for the same reason 'load' and 'freight' were dropped from BS-031, and 'number' was dropped after a probe on 'the card carries an account number'. Known accepted boundary: 'the frame carries the image' fires, and a picture frame arguably does that literally, though 'holds' is the verb English actually uses there. Subject nouns for stocked retail (store, shop) are excluded so the 'carries that brand' sense cannot match. Extended 2026-09-17 with abstract process and project nouns as subjects (rebuild, redesign, rollout, migration, project, initiative, effort, process, method, approach, decision, change, pivot, experiment, pilot, study, analysis, review), after 'The rebuild carries the argument' came back clean: the object was already on the list and only the subject head was missing. The object list was deliberately NOT extended in that round, which is what keeps the ordinary business and legal register out - 'carries risk', 'carries a cost', 'carries weight', 'carries a penalty' and 'carries consequences' all stay clean.
regex_structures.fix: Say what the artifact does, or give the sentence a person. 'Each board carries its own title, rule and legend' is 'Each board has its own title, rule and legend.' 'Slide 18 carries the business model' is 'Slide 18 is where the business model gets spoken.' 'The margin rail carries the tags' is 'The tags sit in a margin rail on the right.'
regex_structures.research_basis: In-the-wild report (2026-08-10) from the design project that produced BS-031, BS-038 and BS-039. Six sentences of exactly this shape, drawn from that project's own working documents, were run against the deployed checker and returned prohibitions_clear with zero findings: BS-031's object list covers 'the weight' but not 'its own title', which is the form design writing actually produces. Verified 0 of 16 false positives on the genuine-human eval corpus and 0 of 19 on constructed literal-carry probes.

regex_structures.name: stale_figure_of_speech
regex_structures.description: Orwell's first rule, mechanized on a closed list: a figure of speech the reader is used to seeing in print, which has stopped producing an image and now only fills the slot where a plain statement belongs. 'It moves the needle on readiness', 'the federal purse would feel it', 'the low-hanging fruit', 'the tip of the iceberg', 'a double-edged sword', 'many moving parts', 'the lion's share'. This is house style, not an authorship signal: human writing reaches for these constantly, which is the whole reason Orwell wrote the rule, and the eval corpus is therefore not evidence either way. It sits in this file because the mechanism is a fixed phrase set, the same shape as BS-036. Two guards keep the literal senses out: 'raise the bar' matches only when terminal or followed by for/on/across, so 'raised the bar three inches' passes, and 'at the end of the day' matches only in the filler frame (comma, then a subject and a copula or 'comes down to'), so the time-of-day reading passes. Known accepted boundary: a literal high-jump 'raised the bar for the next attempt' fires. 'Guardrail' was considered and rejected: it is ordinary technical vocabulary in AI-safety writing, not a dead metaphor.
regex_structures.fix: Say the thing the figure is standing in for, with the number or the name if you have one. 'It moves the needle on readiness' is 'It shortens the release plan by a day and a half.' 'The federal purse would feel it' is 'It would show up in the CSC budget.' If the image is doing real work and you chose it deliberately, justify it and keep it.
regex_structures.research_basis: Orwell, 'Politics and the English Language' (1946), rule 1, adopted 2026-08-10 from a case-study copy gate that had been running the Orwell pass by hand alongside this server. The list is the set of figures that gate kept catching after the checker had already cleared the text. Judgment-only Orwell rules (cut every word that can go, prefer the active) and the domain-jargon carve-out are in self_review.json and lexical_patterns.orwell; see caveats.jargon_substitution_loses_meaning.

regex_structures.name: conjoined_candour_disclaimer
regex_structures.description: The first-person candour beat appended to the clause it follows: 'The redesign took nine months, and I'm not going to pretend that was the plan.' A performed admission that costs the writer nothing, placed where it reads as earned honesty. Conjoined relative of BS-017, which matches only the two-sentence form (a disclaiming sentence then a short 'But ...' reversal) and whose auxiliary list excludes 'am not going to'. Scoped to the CONJOINED form only: a comma plus and/but must precede the frame. That guard is what distinguishes it from the 2026-07-25 rejection of 'Here's the thing' and 'Let's be honest' as register-dependent traps. Sentence-initial 'I'm not going to pretend I understand the tax code.' is an ordinary hedge qualifying a claim and stays unflagged; the tell is the appending, where the beat attaches to a finished statement to add a note of candour. Accepts straight and curly apostrophes.
regex_structures.fix: Cut the beat and let the statement stand, or replace it with the thing you are declining to pretend about. 'It shipped late, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.' -> 'It shipped late.' or 'It shipped six weeks late, and the cause was ours.' If the admission is real, name it; if it is not, the clause is performing candour rather than doing it.
regex_structures.research_basis: In-the-wild report (2026-09-17); design doc docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-17-candour-frame-and-carry-widening-design.md.

regex_structures.name: copula_avoidance
regex_structures.description: The copula dodge: the model will not write 'is', so it reaches for 'serves as' or 'stands as'. 'The report serves as a guide.' is 'The report is a guide.' Named independently by Wikipedia's editor guide, the tropes.fyi community list and the slop-sense pattern set, which estimates the substitute carries meaning the copula would not in roughly one case in ten. The wider verb family (functions as, operates as, comprises, encompasses, constitutes, resides, features) is DELIBERATELY excluded: a rejection probe found 8/8 of their uses legitimate ('the capacitor functions as a filter', 'the clinic operates as a charity', 'the board comprises seven members'), because those verbs carry technical, legal and organisational senses the copula cannot replace. Only 'serves as' and 'stands as' have no competing sense, the same discipline that dropped 'load' and 'freight' from BS-031. The FP guard is a role-object exclusion over a three-token window, because a person holding an office is ordinary English and the role word is often not adjacent to the determiner ('She stood as the Labour candidate in 2019.'). The electoral sense of 'stands as' falls under the same list.
regex_structures.fix: Use 'is'. 'The report serves as a guide' is 'The report is a guide.' 'The building stands as a monument to the era' is 'The building is a monument to the era', or better, say what it actually does now. Keep the substitute only where it carries meaning 'is' does not.
regex_structures.research_basis: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing (copula avoidance); slop-sense pattern 09; tropes.fyi 'serves as dodge'; survey of 2026-09-17.

regex_structures.name: significance_predicate
regex_structures.description: The other half of the copula dodge, where the substitute verb also inflates the claim: 'represents / marks / embodies / exemplifies' plus a determiner and an evaluative abstract noun ('a shift', 'a pivotal moment', 'the culmination', 'a commitment'). Both ends are closed lists, which keeps the literal senses clean: 'the graph represents the data', 'the lawyer represents the defendant', 'the symbol represents hydrogen', 'the line marks the boundary' and 'the union represents four thousand workers' all pass, because no concrete object is on the list. Overlaps BS-004 significance_puffery at the edges; BS-004 matches four fixed strings, this matches the frame.
regex_structures.fix: Say what changed and for whom. 'It represents a shift in how the team works' is 'The team now reviews before merging, which it did not do in March.' If the significance is real, the fact carries it.
regex_structures.research_basis: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing (undue emphasis on significance; copula avoidance); survey of 2026-09-17.

regex_structures.name: signposted_conclusion
regex_structures.description: The announced ending: 'In conclusion', 'To sum up', 'In summary', 'To conclude', 'In closing', 'All in all'. The reader can see the piece ending; saying so spends a sentence on navigation. Legitimate in academic and formal report writing, which is why the gate is checklist rather than hard. Boundary-anchored, so 'he wrote a summary of the meeting' and 'she gave it in summary form' never match.

detection.pattern: (?:^|[.!?]\s+|\n)[ \t]*(?:\*\*)?(?:in conclusion|to sum up|to summarise|to summarize|in summary|to conclude|in closing|all in all)\b[,:]?

regex_structures.fix: Cut the signpost and state the last point. If the closing paragraph needs an announcement to read as closing, it is not closing anything.
regex_structures.research_basis: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing; tropes.fyi 'signposted conclusion'; survey of 2026-09-17.

regex_structures.name: staccato_negation_triple
regex_structures.description: The staccato negation run: 'Not a bug. Not a feature. A fundamental design flaw.' Two consecutive Not-initial fragments, usually resolved by a third. Distinct from BS-013 (the two-sentence copula flip) and BS-039 (the single-sentence 'Not because X, but because Y'), both of which are two-limb and return nothing here. The FP guard is a REQUIRED DETERMINER (a/an/the/just), which is what separates the machine version from ordinary human emphasis: 'Not now. Not ever.' and 'Not bad. Not great.' are adverbial and pass.
regex_structures.fix: Say the thing once, in a full sentence. 'Not a bug. Not a feature. A fundamental design flaw.' is 'This is a design flaw, not a bug.'
regex_structures.research_basis: tropes.fyi 'Not X. Not Y. Just Z.'; survey of 2026-09-17.

regex_structures.name: analogy_invitation
regex_structures.description: The instructed analogy: 'Think of it as a Swiss Army knife for your workflow.' The reader is told to hold a comparison rather than shown why it fits, and the comparison is usually generic enough to drop into any topic. Boundary-anchored and determiner-scoped, so mid-sentence uses ('I think of it as home'), the unrelated 'Think of the children' and quoted dialogue all pass.
regex_structures.fix: Give the comparison a job or cut it. If the analogy explains something the plain description does not, make the mapping explicit; otherwise describe the thing.
regex_structures.research_basis: tropes.fyi 'Think of it as...'; survey of 2026-09-17.

regex_structures.name: structure_announcement
regex_structures.description: Announcing the procedure instead of performing it: 'Let's break this down', 'Let's unpack', 'Let's dive into', 'Let's walk through'. Sibling of BS-022 meta_label, which catches the standalone label form. These announce PROCEDURE, which is what separates them from the 2026-07-25 rejection of 'Let's be honest' and 'Here's the thing' as register-dependent stance markers. 'Let's explore' was cut from the list during the build as too close to ordinary collaborative writing.
regex_structures.fix: Delete the announcement and do the thing. The next paragraph is the breakdown; saying it is coming adds a sentence and no information.
regex_structures.research_basis: tropes.fyi "Let's break this down"; survey of 2026-09-17.

regex_structures.name: boasts_feature_brag
regex_structures.description: 'boasts a/an/over X' as an inflated copula: the marketing brag that replaces 'has'. Scoped to the collocation 2026-09-18 after the bare lexicon entry measured 7.4 per 10k on long-form human prose, where 'boast' is an ordinary verb of vanity ('a man not given to boast of his courage').
regex_structures.fix: Use 'has', 'offers', 'includes' or 'comes with', or state the feature without the verb.

regex_structures.name: elevate_your_x
regex_structures.description: 'elevate your X' and 'elevate the experience/brand/conversation': the marketing intensifier for 'improve'. Scoped to the collocation 2026-09-18 after the bare lexicon entry measured 7.4 per 10k on long-form human prose, where 'elevate' is literal ('the engineers elevated the track above the river').
regex_structures.fix: Say what actually improves and by how much: 'raise', 'lift', 'improve', or name the change.

regex_structures.name: metaphorical_landscape
regex_structures.description: 'the digital/competitive/evolving landscape' and 'the landscape is shifting': the metaphor that names a field without describing it. Scoped to the collocation 2026-09-18 after the bare lexicon entry measured 6.8 per 10k on long-form human prose, where 'landscape' is literal geography. The lexicon entry already said 'flagged when used metaphorically'; this mechanizes that note.
regex_structures.fix: Name the field and the change: 'the market', 'the field', 'what buyers now expect', with the specific shift.

regex_structures.name: time_noun_as_agent
regex_structures.description: A time, calendar or activity noun as the agent of a survival, predation or possession verb: 'the Fridays survived', 'Busy season eats the Fridays', 'Billiards survives final year', 'Work does not get to claim them'. The schedule becomes a creature and the person who decides disappears. Added 2026-09-29 from a B2 worksheet exemplar that passed the checker clean while a reviewer flagged all four. Three scoped branches, each anchored at a clause, line, cell or list-item start: a weekday, weekend, part-of-day, semester or compound-season subject whose verb is followed by a determiner, an object pronoun or the sentence end; a noun subject with third-person 'survives final year / the semester' (so 'I survived the semester' passes); and 'work/school/the job does not get to claim'. Bare seasons are excluded ('the winter killed the roses' is literal), and so are 'Mondays kill me', 'steal up on', 'died away', the passive 'claimed by', compounds and headings ('Weekend eats: five brunch spots', 'Saturday claims are processed') and 'claimed two lives'. Sibling of BS-031 and the abstraction-as-agent rubric item (AP-033, AP-044).
regex_structures.fix: Name the person as the actor and say what happens: 'I still make it to billiards on Fridays', 'No billiards from January to April', 'I keep billiards every second Friday through final year'.

regex_structures.name: clipped_retention_verdict
regex_structures.description: A two-to-six-word sentence of the form [noun phrase] + stays/goes + full stop, performing a decision in executive-summary cadence: 'The Scouts books and the tutoring stay.', 'Tutoring stays.'. Added 2026-09-29 from the same worksheet exemplar. Fires only when the verb ends the sentence, so 'The car stays in the garage.' passes. Declined: pronoun, quantifier and adverb subjects in any case ('He stays.', 'No one stays.', 'Few stay.', 'Please stay.', 'So it goes.', 'As the saying goes.'), a name after a title ('Mr. Darcy stays.'), and a determiner or modal before the verb ('his stay.'). 'remains' is left out on purpose: 'Questions remain.' and 'The chapel remains.' are ordinary prose. Known residual: a literal 'The dog stays.' still fires, since nothing short of semantics separates it from the verdict. Budgeted at one per document, because the repeated verdict is the stronger tell.
regex_structures.fix: Say who is doing what: 'I am keeping the Scouts books and the tutoring.', '...and keep tutoring my Grade 9 student.'

regex_structures.name: deictic_stance_closer
regex_structures.description: A clause-final 'and I want to keep it there / keep it that way' pointing back at a number already named in the same sentence ('Seven to eight hours of sleep, and I want to keep it there.'). It adds no fact and performs resolve; a performative framing beat in the AP-035 family. Added 2026-09-29. Requires a number earlier in the sentence and the sentence end right after 'there' or 'that way', so 'keep it simple', 'keep it there until Tuesday', 'keep it up' and the literal 'the key is under the mat and I want to keep it there' pass. The bare 'I want to keep it that way' after a state with no number is left to the rubric: it is common human speech.
regex_structures.fix: Cut the closer and use the space for a new concrete fact: 'Most of my stress right now comes from co-op applications.'

regex_structures.name: time_back_refrain
regex_structures.description: 'get/have my [time noun] back' ('I get my Fridays back in May', 'I have my evenings back'). Ordinary once; repeated in one piece it becomes a refrain, which is what a second review pass flagged on 2026-09-29. Budget-only: single instances are not reported, and the checker emits one document_budget finding with every instance's excerpt when the count exceeds one. 'got my money back' and 'her back to the wall' do not match.
regex_structures.fix: Keep one and state the other plainly: 'Billiards starts again in May.'

regex_structures.name: graded_contrast_like
regex_structures.description: The graded comparison 'less like X and more like Y' ('The role is less like a manager and more like a translator.'). It recasts a plain description as a corrected misconception. Only the 'like ... like' form is reported per instance, because it fired nowhere in long-form human prose, pre-2022 essays or pre-2022 Wikipedia. The 'less about ... more about' form is ordinary once and is budgeted separately as BS-057. Scoped to one clause: a sentence end, semicolon, colon or line break between the halves stops the match, so 'Nothing is less like home. More like a hotel.' does not fire.
regex_structures.fix: Say what the thing is: 'Most of the job is translating between the two teams.' If the contrast is the point, name the misconception you are correcting and who holds it.
regex_structures.research_basis: Graphite, 'AI Tells' (Druck, Paredes and Smith, 16 Sep 2026; an industry study, not peer-reviewed): 'less like a _ and more like' at 82 to 105 times the rate in 10k pre-ChatGPT human articles for Claude Opus 5, rising as hype vocabulary declines. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

regex_structures.name: graded_contrast_about
regex_structures.description: 'less about X and more about Y' ('It's less about speed and more about trust.'). Budget-only: a single use is ordinary human writing (three in Paul Graham's essays, e.g. 'less about ancientness and more about texts'), so single instances are not reported and only a second use in one piece is, as a document_budget finding with both excerpts. The per-instance 'like' form is BS-056.
regex_structures.fix: Keep the one that carries a real correction and state the others directly.
regex_structures.research_basis: Graphite, 'AI Tells' (Druck, Paredes and Smith, 16 Sep 2026; an industry study, not peer-reviewed), as BS-056. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

regex_structures.name: chatbot_residue
regex_structures.description: Assistant meta-talk left in a draft, on a narrow list: 'Certainly!' or 'Absolutely!' introducing a text artifact ('Certainly! Here is a revised summary'), a sentence-initial 'As an AI language model, I', 'as of my last knowledge cutoff', 'Here's a polished/rewritten version', and 'Would you like me to expand on / elaborate on / adjust the tone'. Each surviving branch is meta-talk that only makes sense addressed to the person who requested the text. Dropped because human email and Slack use them as ordinary courtesy: 'I hope this helps', 'You're absolutely right', 'I'd be happy to help', 'Let me know if you'd like me to', 'Great question', 'Sure! / Of course! Here's the Zoom link', 'Here's the updated/revised draft of the lease', 'Would you like me to make any changes before it goes to print?'. 'As an AI' needs a comma and then 'I', because 'They read as an AI tell' (this server's own sibling prompt, which the first draft fired on) and 'As an AI researcher, I' are ordinary. Narrowed before shipping by an independent adversarial review (2026-10-30).
regex_structures.fix: Delete it. Nothing addressed to the person who asked for the text belongs in the text.
regex_structures.research_basis: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing (WP:CERTAINLY, communication intended for the user); Sun, Yin, Xu, Kolter and Liu, 'Idiosyncrasies in Large Language Models' (ICML 2025): ChatGPT characteristically opens with 'certainly' and 'below is'. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

regex_structures.name: fiction_stock_phrase
regex_structures.description: Narrative stock phrases that most current models over-produce relative to human fiction, on a closed list of full collocations: '(voice) barely above a whisper', 'voice trembling slightly', 'heart hammering against his ribs' or 'pounding in her chest', 'the air thick with the scent of', 'eyes never leaving', 'casting long shadows', 'a smile playing on her lips', and the default character names Elara and Kael. Possessives are third person only, because 'I woke with my heart pounding in my chest' is memoir and health-forum English. 'Pauline Kael' and 'Kael'thas' are excluded. Removed after review because they are everyday idioms outside fiction: 'couldn't shake the feeling' ('I couldn't shake the feeling I'd left the stove on'), 'a profound sense of' (condolence statements), 'barely audible' (bug reports) and 'thick with the smell of' (protest reporting). Never added: 'took a deep breath' and 'something else entirely'. Narrowed before shipping by an independent adversarial review (2026-10-30).
regex_structures.fix: Replace the stock image with what this character in this scene would actually do or notice: 'She could hardly get the words out.' Rename a default-named character.
regex_structures.research_basis: Paech, Roush, Goldfeder and Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop' (arXiv 2510.15061, 2025), Table 5, share of 67 models whose top over-represented trigrams include the pattern: 'voice barely whisper' 68.7%, 'air thick scent' 49.3%, 'smile playing lips' 43.3%, 'could shake feeling' 31.3%, 'eyes never leaving' 29.9%, 'casting long shadows' 28.4%, 'heart pounding chest' 25.4%; Table 1: 'Elara' 85,513x and 'heart hammered ribs' 1,192x in gemma-3-12b. Chakrabarty, Laban and Wu (CHI 2025): cliche is about a sixth of 8,035 professional edits to LLM fiction. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

regex_structures.name: abstract_emotion_frame
regex_structures.description: Emotion named as an inventory instead of shown: 'a mix of pride and sadness', 'a strange blend of relief and dread', 'the weight of the unspoken'. Known accepted boundary: reaction-story journalism writes 'greeted the verdict with a mix of relief and anger', which fires; the evidence is from fiction, so the rule ships at low confidence. The mix frame needs an emotion noun on both sides of 'and', so 'a mix of flour and sugar' and 'a blend of tea and spices' pass. Bare 'a sense of' and 'felt a sense of' were rejected: they fire on human prose in every corpus ('feel a sense of urgency', 'felt a sense of injury').
regex_structures.fix: Show the two feelings through what the person does or says: 'She was proud of him, and it made her sad.'
regex_structures.research_basis: Chakrabarty, Laban and Wu, 'Can AI writing be salvaged?' (CHI 2025): 'weight of', 'sense of' and 'mix of' occur rarely or never in the human seed paragraphs but often in GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Llama 3.1 70B output; professional writers edited the 'a mix of' pattern 54 percent of the time; 'unspoken' appears in about 15 percent of responses. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

regex_structures.name: corrective_framing_disclaimer
regex_structures.description: A disclaimer that corrects a reading nobody proposed, or flags the limits of its sources: 'Claims about its floating should be treated as religious tradition rather than as archaeological explanation', 'Her early life is not widely documented', 'based on the provided sources', 'in the provided context'. The 'treated as X rather than as Y' frame needs an evidentiary adjective on the Y side (historical, archaeological, scientific, factual, documented, established, verified, literal, empirical, definitive, authoritative), because legal and academic prose writes 'should be read as a limitation rather than as a grant of authority' and 'should be interpreted as exploratory rather than as confirmatory'. The source-gap branch keeps only 'provided', the retrieval-assistant word: 'Based on the available information, police believe' and 'no mention in the available sources before 1650' are police and historiography boilerplate. 'does not establish that' was never added. Narrowed before shipping by an independent adversarial review (2026-10-30).
regex_structures.fix: State what is known and stop: 'Local tradition says the stone floats; no survey has examined it.' If a source gap matters, name the source that is missing.
regex_structures.research_basis: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing (2024-26 source-gap phrasing, and corrective disclaimers described as nearly absent from AI output before July 2026); Graphite, 'AI Tells' (Druck, Paredes and Smith, 16 Sep 2026; an industry study, not peer-reviewed): corrective framing at about 12 times the human rate in GPT-6 Astra. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

regex_structures.name: optimistic_future_closer
regex_structures.description: The forward-looking wrap-up in the final paragraph: 'As the field/industry/technology continues to evolve, ...', 'Looking ahead, ...' with no date, number, weekday or relative day ('tonight', 'tomorrow', 'this weekend') in the sentence, 'One thing is clear:', 'the future of X looks bright'. Scoped to the last paragraph by a lookahead that walks to the end of the text and fails at the next blank line followed by content, so the same phrase in the body passes; carriage returns count as blank-line whitespace, so Windows line endings work. The lookahead uses possessive quantifiers (Python 3.11 and later; the image runs 3.12), which keep a body packed with candidate phrases linear per match: a plain lookahead took 3.3 seconds at the 100k-character input cap. A one-paragraph text is its own last paragraph, so run it on the assembled document. Removed after review: 'only time will tell' and 'remains to be seen' (neutral wire-story and review endings, not upbeat summaries), and any subject of 'continues to grow' outside a short list of abstract nouns ('As the plant continues to grow, move it to a larger pot'). Known gaps: a signature or sign-off after the closer counts as the last paragraph and hides it, and text whose paragraphs are separated by single newlines is treated as one paragraph. Narrowed before shipping by an independent adversarial review (2026-10-30). Widened 2026-11-09 to spare weekdays and relative days, after the terse-register set showed 'Looking ahead, the forecast calls for rain through Thursday.' firing. The same day the date guard was bounded to the next 200 characters of the sentence: unbounded, it rescanned the rest of the sentence for every candidate and took 9.6 seconds at the 100k-character input cap on text with no full stops.
regex_structures.fix: End on the last concrete fact: 'The council votes in March.' Cut the forecast unless it has a date or a number in it.
regex_structures.research_basis: Russell, Karpinska and Iyyer, 'People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text' (ACL 2025): conclusions are 13.1 percent of the clues expert annotators cite; AI endings are 'repetitive and overly optimistic summaries' while human ones 'end more abruptly and less tidily'. Graphite, 'AI Tells' (Druck, Paredes and Smith, 16 Sep 2026; an industry study, not peer-reviewed): 'looking ahead the' 33x. Tian et al. (EMNLP 2024): LLM stories are homogeneously positive. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

regex_structures.name: importance_flag
regex_structures.description: A sentence that announces that something matters instead of showing the consequence: 'This distinction matters because ...', 'Knowing which type you have matters more than most beginners realize', and the heading 'Why this matters'. Scoped to a sentence-initial demonstrative or a short list of meta nouns (distinction, difference, point, detail, choice, order, framing, nuance), or to 'matters more than [people] realize/think'. 'It matters very little now', 'What matters is ...' (BS-015) and 'may matter more than outsiders think' (no third-person 'matters') pass, and 'The order matters here: auth middleware must run first' was taken out after review, because technical docs use it as a real warning. Accepted boundary: the personal-finance headline 'Your credit score matters more than you think' fires.
regex_structures.fix: Give the consequence and drop the announcement: 'Teams mix the two up, and then the audit fails.'
regex_structures.research_basis: Graphite, 'AI Tells' (Druck, Paredes and Smith, 16 Sep 2026; an industry study, not peer-reviewed): 'matters because' at 132x (Claude Opus 5) and 357x (GPT-6 Astra), 'matters more than' 93x, 'distinction matters' absent from the human corpus. Also observed in a default-style Claude Sonnet sample generated for this round. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

regex_structures.name: as_much_about_aphorism
regex_structures.description: The balanced aphorism 'X is as much about A as B' ('Gardening is as much about patience as technique.', 'Leadership is as much a matter of listening as speaking.'), usually a closer that restates the piece as a maxim, so it is scoped to the last paragraph with the BS-062 lookahead; the stock review sentence in the body ('The film is as much about the city as it is about the people who leave it') passes. Contractions count ('It's as much about patience as technique'). A sibling of BS-018 copula_maxim_closer. 'ate as much as I could' and 'costs as much as a car' pass, because the frame needs 'as much about' or 'as much a matter of' after a copula.
regex_structures.fix: Cut it, or replace the maxim with the specific claim it summarises.
regex_structures.research_basis: Russell et al. (ACL 2025) on tidy, summarising conclusions. Observed closing a default-style Claude Sonnet sample generated for this round, with 0 matches in long-form human prose, pre-2022 essays and pre-2022 Wikipedia against an 'as much' control that fires in all three. Research round 2026-10-30 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-30-research-round-academic-tells.md).

alternatives.notes: Travel-brochure register ('nestled in the heart of the valley'). Sibling of 'bustling' and 'hidden gem'.
Promotional intensifier from the Wikipedia signs-of-AI list (2026-09-17). Almost always reachable by a plainer word or by the fact itself.
Unearned prestige marker; pairs with 'boasts' and 'nestled' in generated travel and profile copy.

alternatives: or name what people could see or hear

alternatives.notes: Scoped to the collocation, not bare 'diverse', which is an ordinary word. Same discipline as 'hidden gem'.
Promotional cliche from the Wikipedia signs-of-AI list. Multi-word, matched verbatim.

alternatives: or show what the person does
or just state it simply without the preamble
or just conclude without announcing it
or just summarize without announcing it

credibility.description: AI-assisted writing often vouches for the authenticity of its own account by repeatedly insisting it is real, actual, genuine, or true. A human rarely needs to insist their own work is real; the insistence is a defensive credibility hedge, and the DENSITY of the token set across a document is the tell, not any single use.
credibility.ai_pattern: The same reality-asserting lemma recurs throughout a piece ('a real engagement', 'the real one', 'the design is real', 'the real flow'). Each use passes any single-token check, but the repetition reads as a writer arguing for their own credibility.
credibility.human_pattern: Human writers let the specifics carry credibility. They name the client, the constraint, the date, the artifact, and almost never label their own account 'real'. When they do, it is once, for a genuine contrast.
exclusions: one sentence-initial 'actually' as a discourse marker
rewriting_guidance: If one of these tokens appears three or more times, cut all but at most one. The narrative detail should establish that the work is real; you should not have to say so.
Replace the assertion with the specific that justified it: not 'a real engagement' but 'a live, mid-build engagement'; not 'the real flow' but 'the flow the operators actually follow'.
Keep a single use only where it draws a genuine contrast (e.g. real versus hypothetical), and make that contrast explicit.
credibility.research_basis: proposed-rules PR2-#1; in-the-wild audit of nicojan.com/work/art-studio-blueprint (2026-06-28), where seven uses of 'real' in ~1,500 words passed the checker clean.

self_review: AR-001 — meaning preserved: confirm claims, numbers, names, and stance are unchanged from the source, and the tone the user asked for is intact.

Rhythm: read the draft in your head — do sentence lengths and shapes vary, or march at one cadence? Break up runs of same-length sentences; add a short fragment or a longer multi-clause sentence. (Burstiness is auto-measured; this is the qualitative read.)

Reused rhetorical shape: the same construction — an antithesis ('not X, but Y'), a copula maxim, a rule-of-three — restated across the piece reads as a tic even when the words differ. Vary the constructions, not just the vocabulary. The budget for the shapes that carry one ('at most one antithesis', 'at most one appended label', 'at most one aphorism') is a budget for the WHOLE PIECE, and checking section by section cannot enforce it: four sections can each pass with one instance while the document holds four. Count these across every section, and run the last humanizer_check_text on the assembled document, not only on the part you edited last. The four mechanized shapes (BS-011, BS-018, BS-038, BS-039) are now counted automatically and reported as a document_budget finding, but only within the text handed to the checker, so the last run still has to be on the assembled document. The shapes in this item that no detector can find are yours to count. See caveats.per_section_checks_miss_document_budgets.

Contrastive 'X, not Y' outside the copula frame: BS-011 fires only on a copula plus a clause-final Y, so "We chose depth, not breadth." and "The wordmark comes from paint on paper, not the polished apps she gave up on." are yours to judge. One contrast is ordinary writing; the tell is the reflex, the same binary reached for in section after section. Count them across the whole piece, and rewrite the repeats as a positive claim that stands on its own. See caveats.contrastive_scope_notes_are_the_same_shape.

Section-to-section variation: does the style shift between sections, or hold one flat fingerprint throughout? Humans modulate; LLMs stay even. Make one section terse and another more flowing. (Cross-section uniformity is auto-detected; this is the qualitative read.)

Generic competence and stance: could this have been written about almost any topic, by almost anyone? Cut smooth-but-empty phrasing, reflexive hedges, and motivational closers. Commit to a real point of view and at least one concrete, specific, checkable detail.

Abstraction-as-agent: an abstract noun ('the gap', 'the work', 'the craft', 'the order') used as the subject of an agentive or experiential verb (mattered, decided, kept, taught, carries, carried, holds, demands) reads fluent but no one is actually doing anything. Metaphorical 'carry' is the most frequent instance and the hardest to hear ('the layout carries the weight', 'the silence carried the room', 'eight words to carry'): the verb performs gravity while the sentence names no actor and no effect. Prefer a human or concrete subject, and say what the thing actually does. The fixed collocations are auto-detected as BS-031; the open-ended abstract-subject cases are this rubric item (server cannot verify reliably; see AP-033, AP-044). Time and calendar nouns count too, and they are the hardest to hear because they read as a lively figure: 'the Fridays survived', 'Busy season eats the Fridays', 'Billiards survives final year', 'Work does not get to claim them'. The weekday, semester and season frames are mechanized as BS-052 at low confidence; read for the rest, such as a schedule, a job or an activity that 'decides', 'wins' or 'gives back'. Fix: name the person and say what happens ('I still make it to billiards on Fridays'). Ideas and artifacts slip in the same way, most often inside a maxim about the work: 'the answer usually costs you the design you arrived with', 'A design that ignores the build comes back', 'the only thing I do that asks me to stand still'. A reviewer flagged all three on a portfolio site in 2026; none has a lexical anchor the checker could use.

Performative framing beat: a sentence or label whose real job is to perform insight, closure, or self-awareness rather than carry content. Three forms — (a) a self-satisfied closer: a neat aphorism ending a section that adds no new fact, name, or number, often crediting the author or pivoting on a tidy antithesis ('The data set is public; the reading of it is mine.'); (b) first-person meta-commentary on the work itself ('my take', 'the reading of it is mine', 'as I see it') in a piece meant to be evidence-led; (c) a clever paradox headline used to sound sharp where a plain statement of the point would do. Delete the beat and end on the last substantive point. Keep at most one aphoristic or paradox construction per piece, and only where it does analytical work — the device is human in moderation; the tell is repetition and substitution for content. The standalone meta-label form ('in 200 words', 'in brief') is auto-detected as BS-022; the closer overlaps BS-018; see AP-035, AP-033. Short cells and captions have their own versions: the clipped verdict that performs a decision ('Tutoring stays.', BS-053), the stance closer that points back at a number already given ('and I want to keep it there', BS-054), and the tidy aphoristic closer that rounds off a plain list ('four months is a long time to wait', 'tires me out more than any lecture did'). Replace each with the next concrete fact. Captions have a numeric version, the verbless pair that sets one against many ('One count, four moments', 'Three sizes, all the same height.', 'One app, every chat.'). It could not be mechanized: 'Two adults, one child.', 'Two tablets, every four hours.' and 'Three goals, one assist.' are the same shape in ordinary terse writing (see AP-069). A maxim that hands the verdict to a third party is the same beat ('and the developer is right to send it back').

Excessive coherence and tidiness: does every point line up too neatly — each example fitting perfectly, every thread resolved, no loose ends or tension left? Real human writing has friction: a caveat that complicates the thesis, a digression, an example that only mostly fits, a point left partly open. Seamless, frictionless argument is itself a tell. Add back the messiness the topic actually has.

Appended significance label: a heading, subtitle or dek that names its subject and then annexes a second element promising the subject matters — a reduced relative ('Reintegration support at the moment of release, and the officer the whole system turns on.'), an appositive that asserts a hinge, or a WH clause pre-defending a choice ('Method, and why this one'). Read every label in the piece: does the part after the comma add a fact, or does it only tell the reader this is important? Cut it and let the section earn it. One such label may be deliberate; two or more in one piece is the tell, because a repeated rhetorical shape is what reads as machine-made. The WH form is auto-detected as BS-038; the reduced-relative and appositive forms need a parser the server does not have, so they are this rubric item (see AP-051). Budget: one per document, counted across the assembled whole rather than section by section — the durable signal is the repeated shape, not any single instance, and check_text is stateless (see per_section_checks_miss_document_budgets). The WH form is mechanized as BS-038; the appositive form that appends a reduced relative is not, and three attempts to mechanize it are recorded in labels_are_where_the_tells_hide. Attested forms to read for: 'Reintegration support at the moment of release, and the officer the whole system turns on.', 'The rebuild, and the one decision that made it possible.', 'Nine months of rework, and the meeting that started it.'

Plainness (the Orwell pass, run last): after the other phases are clear, read the draft once more for the three things this server's own layers do not catch, because they are marks of flabby prose rather than of machine authorship. (a) Stale figures of speech: any image you did not choose deliberately ('moves the needle', 'the federal purse', 'the tip of the iceberg'). A closed list is auto-detected as BS-041; the class is open, so read for it. Replace the figure with the number or the name it stood in for, not with a fresher figure. (b) Words that can go: if a word can be cut, cut it. This is the rule that does the most work in anything longer than a page, and the padding phrases in lexical_patterns.orwell.padding_phrases are a starting point, not the rule. (c) The passive where the active will do: name who did it. Deliberately not mechanized, because the legitimate passive is common in method and regulatory writing. One carve-out, and it is not optional: a domain term with no everyday equivalent (statutory release, Protected B, an API, a subpoena) is DEFINED in plain words at first use and then used plainly. Do not substitute a vaguer everyday word for it; that loses the meaning the argument runs on. Then re-run humanizer_check_text, because cutting words changes sentence-length variance. See lexical_patterns.orwell and caveats.jargon_substitution_loses_meaning.

Durable signal: local word-level unpredictability and section-to-section variation are the most human signals and are not measured server-side. Surface word swaps are necessary but not sufficient — do not stop at vocabulary.

Anaphora and repeated sentence openings: three or more consecutive sentences opening on the same word or the same two words ('They assume users will pay. They assume the market is ready. They assume nothing changes.'). Read the run and ask one question: is the repetition doing work, or is it filling space? **The form itself is legitimate and has a name.** Thoreau wrote 'It does not keep the country free. It does not settle the West. It does not educate.', and Melville 'Forty years of continual whaling! Forty years of privation, and peril, and storm-time!' — deliberate anaphora that builds. The tell is the same construction used without escalation, where each limb restates the first instead of advancing it, and where cutting the repetition would cost the passage nothing. That distinction is why this is a rubric item and not a detector: the abusive case and the figure are syntactically identical, and every formulation tried scored 0/15 precision on genuine human prose (see caveats.rhetorical_figures_defeat_shape_detection). Only the This/These/It chain is auto-detected, as BS-009. Budget: at most one deliberate anaphoric run per document, counted across the assembled whole rather than section by section, and it should be the strongest passage in the piece — if it is not, cut it (see caveats.per_section_checks_miss_document_budgets).

Over-explained subtext: does a sentence explain what the image, line or example before it already showed ('He slammed the door. He was angry.')? Professional writers cut this in about a fifth of their edits to LLM drafts, and it does not go away as models improve (Chakrabarty, Laban and Wu, CHI 2025). Cut the explanation and trust the reader.

Reader contact (essays, blog posts, opinion pieces, cover letters, not reference or technical copy): is there a single I, you or question in the whole piece? LLM essays use markedly less interactional language, meaning stance, engagement and questions to the reader, than human ones (Jiang and Hyland, English for Specific Purposes, 2025). Add one only where it carries a real position; never inject it as decoration.

Defaults a reader recognises: quote attributions that rotate through 'notes', 'explains' and 'emphasizes' where a reporter would write 'says' every time; every bullet opening with a bold label and a colon; emoji at the start of headings or bullets; stock names (Emily, Sarah, Dr. Chen, Elara). Expert annotators cite each of these (Russell, Karpinska and Iyyer, ACL 2025). Use the plain form unless the house style asks for the other one.

Cause-to-benefit 'so' tail: a sentence that states a mechanism and then appends ', so' plus the payoff it promises the reader ('Quip updates itself, so a fix reached people within a day of shipping.', 'Only the width changes, so the window stays under the menu-bar icon and nothing jumps away from the pointer.'). It reads as a product brochure explaining its own value. A reviewer flagged both as AI-coded; the shape is too common in plain prose to detect, so read for it. Keep the 'so' when the reader needs the causal link; cut it when the second half only tells them the first half was good. Often the fix is to keep one half: the fact, or the user's experience of it.

Backstory order and self-portrait flourish: lines that tell the writer's history as a tidy sequence or describe their own habits approvingly. Attested, all flagged as AI-coded in a 2026 portfolio and résumé review: 'Ten years of teaching neurodivergent and multilingual learners came first, and so did the habit of watching where people get stuck.', 'Before them came two web tools for English learners.', 'The job was watching someone try to make sense of something complicated...', 'I design the screens, build them in code, and keep the Figma files behind them tidy.', 'People I've never met use it'. Each sounds like a voice performing modesty or craft. State the fact with its date or number ('Teaching neurodivergent and multilingual learners since 2016.') and drop the adjective about yourself. 'X came first, and so did the habit of Y' could not be mechanized, because 'Prices rose, and so did the practice of haggling.' is the same construction.

Cold-reader test for product, portfolio and case-study copy: could someone who has never used the product follow this sentence on first read? Three failures recur, all flagged in a 2026 portfolio review after passing the checker. (a) Mechanism in a chain of clauses instead of what the user gets: 'Show them in every space and they stay at the top of the sidebar, with one sign-in and one unread count, while the rest of the list changes.' (b) The product's own internal words, or verbs users never say: 'cut across all of them', 'Filing a GIF' (nobody files GIFs), 'nothing of the app is drawn inside Chorus'. (c) A slogan whose second half is clever and impossible to picture: 'Every chat and inbox in one Mac window, and only what's new turns red.' Also cut vague casual counts ('a dozen or so testers'), run-in labels ('The worst bug:'), and release-by-release history ('first release 13 July'). Write short sentences in plain words, use a UX term where it is the right term, and define any product concept before using it.
